chunks.heading: What is a mechanical wave?
chunks.body: A mechanical wave is a disturbance that needs a medium, like water or a rope, to travel through. Sound and water waves are both mechanical waves.
chunks.checkText: What does a mechanical wave need in order to travel?

chunks.heading: Waves carry energy, not matter
chunks.body: A [[phys-mechanical-wave|mechanical wave]] moves energy from one place to another. The particles of the medium don't travel with the wave — they just wobble in place.
chunks.checkText: As a wave passes through water, what actually travels forward?

chunks.heading: A single pulse vs a continuous wave
chunks.body: One quick flick of a rope sends a single wave pulse. Shaking the rope again and again instead sends a continuous, repeating wave.
chunks.checkText: What creates a continuous wave rather than a single pulse?

checkOptions.text: Repeated, ongoing shaking of the source

chunks.heading: Transverse waves: side to side
chunks.body: In a transverse wave, the medium's particles move up and down, at right angles to the direction the wave travels. A wave on a string is transverse.
chunks.checkText: In a transverse wave, particles move...

checkOptions.text: Perpendicular to the wave's direction of travel
Parallel to the wave's direction of travel
In a circle around the wave

chunks.heading: Crest and trough
chunks.body: In a [[phys-transverse-wave|transverse wave]], the highest point above the resting position is the crest. The lowest point below it is the trough.
chunks.checkText: The lowest point of a transverse wave is called the...

chunks.heading: Longitudinal waves: back and forth
chunks.body: In a longitudinal wave, the medium's particles move back and forth in the same direction the wave travels. Sound is a longitudinal wave.
chunks.checkText: In a longitudinal wave, particles vibrate...

checkOptions.text: Parallel to the wave's direction of travel
Perpendicular to the wave's direction of travel

chunks.heading: Compression and rarefaction
chunks.body: In a [[phys-longitudinal-wave|longitudinal wave]], a compression is where particles bunch close together. A rarefaction is where particles spread further apart.
chunks.checkText: A compression in a longitudinal wave is a region where particles are...

chunks.heading: Amplitude: how big is the wave?
chunks.body: Amplitude is the maximum distance a particle moves away from its resting position. A bigger amplitude means the wave is carrying more energy.
chunks.checkText: A wave with a larger amplitude is carrying...

chunks.heading: Wavelength: the length of one wave
chunks.body: Wavelength is the distance between two matching points on a wave, like crest to crest. It's usually measured in metres.
chunks.checkText: Wavelength is best described as the distance between...

checkOptions.text: Two matching points on a wave, like crest to crest
The top and bottom of one wave

chunks.heading: Frequency: how often waves arrive
chunks.body: Frequency is the number of complete waves passing a point each second. It's measured in hertz (Hz).
chunks.checkText: Frequency measures...

checkOptions.text: How many complete waves pass a point each second
How far a wave has travelled

chunks.heading: Period: the time for one wave
chunks.body: Period is the time it takes for one complete wave to pass a point. It's the opposite of [[phys-frequency|frequency]] — a short period means a high frequency.
chunks.checkText: A wave with a very short period has a...

chunks.heading: Working out wave speed
chunks.body: A wave's speed equals its [[phys-frequency|frequency]] multiplied by its [[phys-wavelength|wavelength]]. Knowing any two of speed, frequency and wavelength lets you calculate the third.
chunks.checkText: The speed of a wave can be found by...

chunks.heading: Reflecting off a fixed end
chunks.body: When a wave pulse hits a rope end that's tied down, it bounces back flipped upside down. A crest reflects as a trough.
chunks.checkText: When a wave reflects off a fixed end, the pulse comes back...

chunks.heading: Reflecting off a free end
chunks.body: When a wave pulse hits an end that's free to move, it bounces back the same way up. A crest reflects as a crest.
chunks.checkText: At a free end, a reflected wave pulse...

checkOptions.text: Keeps the same orientation as before

chunks.heading: The law of reflection
chunks.body: When any wave bounces off a surface, the angle it arrives at equals the angle it leaves at, both measured from an imaginary line called the normal.
chunks.checkText: The law of reflection states that the angle of incidence...

checkOptions.text: Is always bigger than the angle of reflection
Has no relationship to the angle of reflection

chunks.heading: Refraction: waves change direction
chunks.body: Refraction happens when a wave changes direction because its speed changes as it moves into a different medium. Water waves refract when they move from deep to shallow water.
chunks.checkText: Refraction is caused by a wave...

checkOptions.text: Changing speed as it enters a new medium

chunks.heading: Diffraction: bending around edges
chunks.body: Diffraction is when a wave bends as it passes through a gap or around an obstacle. It's most noticeable when the gap is about the same size as the wavelength.
chunks.checkText: Diffraction is most noticeable when the gap is...

checkOptions.text: About the same size as the wavelength

chunks.heading: Constructive superposition
chunks.body: When two waves meet and their crests line up, their displacements add together to make a bigger wave. This is called constructive superposition.
chunks.checkText: Constructive superposition happens when two waves meet and...

checkOptions.text: Their crests line up, making a bigger wave
They cancel each other out completely

chunks.heading: Destructive superposition
chunks.body: When a wave's crest meets another wave's trough, the two displacements partly or fully cancel out. This is called destructive superposition.
chunks.checkText: Destructive superposition happens when a crest meets a...

chunks.heading: Standing waves
chunks.body: A standing wave forms when two waves of equal frequency travel in opposite directions and overlap. It seems to stay in place, with still points called nodes and points of maximum movement called antinodes.
chunks.checkText: A point on a standing wave that never moves is called a...

chunks.heading: Resonance: pushing at just the right rate
chunks.body: Every object has its own natural vibration rate. Resonance happens when something is pushed at exactly that rate, causing its vibrations to grow much larger.
chunks.checkText: Resonance occurs when an object is driven at...

chunks.heading: Sound is a longitudinal wave
chunks.body: Sound travels as a [[phys-longitudinal-wave|longitudinal wave]], made up of [[phys-compression-rarefaction|compressions and rarefactions]] moving through the air. Vibrating objects, like vocal cords, create these waves.
chunks.checkText: Sound is an example of a...

chunks.heading: Sound needs a medium
chunks.body: Because sound is a [[phys-mechanical-wave|mechanical wave]], it cannot travel through empty space. This is why astronauts can't hear each other shout across the vacuum outside their spacecraft.
chunks.checkText: Sound cannot travel through...

chunks.heading: Pitch depends on frequency
chunks.body: A sound's pitch is set by its [[phys-frequency|frequency]]. A higher frequency sounds higher-pitched, like a bird's chirp compared to a foghorn.
chunks.checkText: A higher-pitched sound has a...

chunks.heading: Loudness depends on amplitude
chunks.body: A sound's loudness is set by its [[phys-amplitude|amplitude]]. More energy in the vibration means a bigger amplitude and a louder sound.
chunks.checkText: A louder sound has a bigger...

chunks.heading: Sound behaves like other waves
chunks.body: Because sound is a wave, it can [[phys-reflection-fixed-end|reflect]] as an echo and [[phys-diffraction|diffract]] around corners. Low-pitched sounds, with longer wavelengths, diffract more than high-pitched sounds.
chunks.checkText: Compared to high-pitched sounds, low-pitched sounds diffract...

checkOptions.text: More, because they have longer wavelengths
Less, because they have longer wavelengths

chunks.heading: Sound intensity
chunks.body: Intensity measures how much sound energy passes through an area each second. It's measured in watts per square metre and roughly matches how loud a sound seems.
chunks.checkText: Sound intensity is measured in...

chunks.heading: Sound fades with distance
chunks.body: As you move away from a sound source, its energy spreads over a bigger area, so intensity drops sharply. Doubling the distance cuts the intensity to one-quarter.
chunks.checkText: If you double your distance from a sound source, the intensity becomes...

chunks.heading: The Doppler effect
chunks.body: The Doppler effect is why a siren sounds higher-pitched as it approaches you and lower-pitched as it moves away. The source's actual frequency never changes — only what you hear does.
chunks.checkText: As an ambulance moves towards you, its siren sounds...

chunks.heading: Beats: two close frequencies clashing
chunks.body: When two sounds of slightly different frequency play together, you hear a regular pulsing volume called beats. Musicians use this to tell when two instruments are almost, but not quite, in tune.
chunks.checkText: Beats are heard when two sounds have...

chunks.heading: Standing waves make musical notes
chunks.body: Instruments like guitars and flutes create [[phys-standing-wave|standing waves]] in strings or air columns. The simplest possible standing wave is the fundamental frequency; the higher ones are called overtones.
chunks.checkText: The simplest, lowest standing wave frequency of an instrument is called its...

chunks.heading: A string fixed at both ends
chunks.body: Both ends of a guitar string are fixed, so they're always [[phys-standing-wave|nodes]]. Its fundamental wavelength is twice the string's length.
chunks.checkText: For a string fixed at both ends, the ends are always...

chunks.heading: A string or tube fixed at one end
chunks.body: If one end is fixed and the other is free, the fixed end is a node and the free end is an antinode. Only odd-numbered harmonics can form this way.
chunks.checkText: In a system fixed at one end only, which harmonics are possible?

chunks.heading: Wind instruments open at both ends
chunks.body: In a pipe open at both ends, like a flute, both ends become antinodes. This works the same way as a [[phys-string-both-ends|string fixed at both ends]].
chunks.checkText: In a pipe open at both ends, the open ends are...

chunks.heading: Wind instruments closed at one end
chunks.body: In a pipe closed at one end, like a clarinet, the closed end is a node and the open end is an antinode. Only odd harmonics are possible, just like a [[phys-string-one-end|string fixed at one end]].
chunks.checkText: In a pipe closed at one end, the closed end is a...

chunks.heading: Light as a straight ray
chunks.body: A simple way to model light is as a straight ray travelling outward from its source. This ray model helps explain how mirrors and lenses form images.
chunks.checkText: In the ray model, light is represented as...

chunks.heading: Images in a flat mirror
chunks.body: A flat mirror forms a virtual image that is upright, the same size as the object, and appears as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.
chunks.checkText: The image formed by a flat mirror is...

checkOptions.text: The same size as the object

chunks.heading: Real image or virtual image?
chunks.body: A real image forms where light rays actually cross, and can be captured on a screen. A virtual image only appears to form, and can only be seen by looking into the mirror or lens.
chunks.checkText: A real image can be...

checkOptions.text: Only seen by looking into the mirror

chunks.heading: Measuring brightness
chunks.body: Luminous intensity, measured in candela, describes how bright a light source is. Like [[phys-inverse-square-sound|sound]], light intensity drops sharply with distance from the source.
chunks.checkText: The unit for luminous intensity is the...

chunks.heading: Refraction of light
chunks.body: Just like any [[phys-refraction-wave|wave]], light bends when it moves between materials where its speed changes, such as from air into water.
chunks.checkText: Light refracts when it...

checkOptions.text: Moves into a material where its speed changes

chunks.heading: Refractive index
chunks.body: The refractive index of a material tells you how much slower light travels in it compared to a vacuum. A higher refractive index means light travels more slowly.
chunks.checkText: A material with a high refractive index causes light to travel...

checkOptions.text: At the same speed as a vacuum

chunks.heading: Snell's law
chunks.body: Snell's law lets you calculate exactly how much a light ray bends when it crosses into a new material, using the refractive indexes of both materials.
chunks.checkText: Snell's law is used to calculate...

checkOptions.text: How much a light ray bends between two materials
How fast a mirror reflects light

chunks.heading: Total internal reflection
chunks.body: When light tries to leave a denser material at a steep enough angle, it can't escape and instead reflects entirely back inside, as though the boundary were a mirror.
chunks.checkText: Total internal reflection happens when light...

checkOptions.text: Cannot escape a denser material and reflects back inside

chunks.heading: The critical angle
chunks.body: The critical angle is the exact angle of incidence where light stops refracting out and instead travels right along the boundary. Beyond this angle, [[phys-total-internal-reflection|total internal reflection]] occurs.
chunks.checkText: At angles greater than the critical angle, light undergoes...

chunks.heading: Dispersion: splitting white light
chunks.body: Dispersion happens because each colour in white light refracts by a slightly different amount. This splits white light into a spectrum of colours, like in a rainbow.
chunks.checkText: Dispersion splits white light into a spectrum because...

checkOptions.text: Each colour refracts by a slightly different amount
All colours always travel at exactly the same speed

chunks.heading: Concave and convex mirrors
chunks.body: A concave mirror curves inward and focuses parallel light rays to a point, so it's called converging. A convex mirror curves outward and spreads light rays apart, so it's called diverging.
chunks.checkText: A mirror that focuses parallel rays to a point is...

chunks.heading: Focal length
chunks.body: The focal length is the distance from a curved mirror to its focus, the point where parallel rays meet. It's half the mirror's radius of curvature.
chunks.checkText: The focal length of a mirror is...

checkOptions.text: Half of its radius of curvature
Equal to its radius of curvature

chunks.heading: Images in a concave mirror
chunks.body: A concave mirror's image changes depending on the object's distance: it can be real and inverted, or if the object is very close, virtual, upright and enlarged.
chunks.checkText: When an object is placed very close to a concave mirror, the image is...

chunks.heading: Images in a convex mirror
chunks.body: A convex mirror always produces a virtual, upright, and smaller image, no matter where the object is placed. This wide view is why they're used as shop security mirrors.
chunks.checkText: A convex mirror always produces an image that is...

chunks.heading: The mirror formula
chunks.body: The mirror formula, 1/f = 1/u + 1/v, connects the focal length, the object's distance and the image's distance, letting you calculate exactly where an image will form.
chunks.checkText: The mirror formula relates focal length to...

checkOptions.text: Only the type of light source

chunks.heading: Magnification
chunks.body: Magnification compares the size of an image to the size of the real object. A magnification of 2 means the image appears twice as tall as the object.
chunks.checkText: A magnification of 0.5 means the image is...

checkOptions.text: Half the size of the object
Twice the size of the object
The same size as the object

chunks.heading: Convex lenses converge light
chunks.body: A convex lens is thicker in the middle than at its edges and bends parallel light rays inward, converging them to a focus, just like a [[phys-curved-mirror-types|concave mirror]].
chunks.checkText: A convex lens is thicker...

checkOptions.text: In the middle than at the edges
At the edges than in the middle

chunks.heading: Concave lenses diverge light
chunks.body: A concave lens is thinner in the middle than at its edges and spreads parallel light rays apart. It always forms a virtual, diminished image.
chunks.checkText: A concave lens always forms an image that is...

chunks.heading: The lens formula
chunks.body: The lens formula, 1/f = 1/u + 1/v, works exactly the same way as the [[phys-mirror-formula|mirror formula]], letting you find where a lens forms its image.
chunks.checkText: The lens formula is...

checkOptions.text: The same equation used for the mirror formula
A completely different equation to the mirror formula

chunks.heading: The kinetic particle model
chunks.body: This model says all matter is made of tiny particles that are always moving. The particles also pull and push on each other with attractive and repulsive forces.
chunks.checkText: According to the kinetic particle model, particles in matter are...

chunks.heading: Particles in a solid
chunks.body: In a solid, strong forces hold particles in roughly fixed positions, though they still vibrate in place. This is why solids keep a fixed shape.
chunks.checkText: Particles in a solid mostly...

chunks.heading: Particles in a gas
chunks.body: In a gas, particles move fast and in random directions, colliding with each other and the container walls. This is why a gas spreads to fill any container.
chunks.checkText: Compared to a solid, particles in a gas...

checkOptions.text: Move much faster and more freely
Move more slowly and stay put

chunks.heading: Heat is not the same as temperature
chunks.body: Heat is the energy transferred from a hotter object to a colder one. Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of a substance's particles.
chunks.checkText: Heat refers to energy that is...

checkOptions.text: Being transferred from hot to cold

chunks.heading: Internal energy
chunks.body: A substance's internal energy is the total kinetic and potential energy of all its particles. Adding heat can raise this energy, which raises temperature or changes state.
chunks.checkText: Internal energy is the total of a substance's particles'...

chunks.heading: Celsius, Fahrenheit and Kelvin
chunks.body: Celsius and Fahrenheit are arbitrary scales based on chosen reference points. The Kelvin scale is absolute, starting at the coldest possible temperature instead of an arbitrary point.
chunks.checkText: Unlike Celsius, the Kelvin scale starts at...

chunks.heading: Absolute zero
chunks.body: Absolute zero is the coldest temperature possible, at 0 kelvin or -273.15 degrees Celsius. At this point, particles have the least possible kinetic energy.
chunks.checkText: Absolute zero occurs at...

chunks.heading: Converting Celsius to kelvin
chunks.body: To change a temperature from Celsius to kelvin, add 273. One degree Celsius is exactly the same size as one kelvin, so the numbers just shift.
chunks.checkText: To convert a Celsius temperature into kelvin, you...

chunks.heading: Thermal equilibrium
chunks.body: Two objects in thermal contact reach thermal equilibrium once energy stops flowing between them. At that point, they are at the same temperature.
chunks.checkText: Two objects are in thermal equilibrium when...

checkOptions.text: Energy has stopped flowing between them
One is much hotter than the other
They are touching but never exchange energy

chunks.heading: The first law of thermodynamics
chunks.body: This law says a system's internal energy changes by the heat added to it minus the work it does. Energy is never created or destroyed, only moved or converted.
chunks.checkText: According to the first law of thermodynamics, energy...

checkOptions.text: Changes form but is never created or destroyed

chunks.heading: Specific heat capacity
chunks.body: Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise 1 kilogram of a material by 1 degree. Water has a high specific heat capacity, so it heats up slowly.
chunks.checkText: A material with a high specific heat capacity...

checkOptions.text: Takes a lot of energy to heat up

chunks.heading: Latent heat: hidden energy
chunks.body: Latent heat is the energy absorbed or released when a substance changes state, like melting or boiling. While this happens, temperature stays constant even though energy keeps being added.
chunks.checkText: While a substance is changing state, its temperature...

chunks.heading: Latent heat of fusion
chunks.body: The latent heat of fusion is the energy needed to melt a solid into a liquid, without changing its temperature. The same amount of energy is released when it re-freezes.
chunks.checkText: The latent heat of fusion is the energy needed to...

checkOptions.text: Melt a solid into a liquid
Boil a liquid into a gas

chunks.heading: Latent heat of vaporisation
chunks.body: The latent heat of vaporisation is the energy needed to turn a liquid into a gas. It usually takes much more energy than melting the same substance, because bonds are broken completely.
chunks.checkText: Compared to melting, boiling a substance usually needs...

chunks.heading: Evaporation and cooling
chunks.body: Evaporation happens when the fastest, highest-energy particles escape a liquid's surface. This leaves the remaining liquid with lower average energy, cooling it down.
chunks.checkText: Evaporation cools a liquid because the particles that escape are...

chunks.heading: Conduction
chunks.body: Conduction is heat transfer through direct contact between particles, without the particles themselves moving from place to place. Metals conduct heat especially well.
chunks.checkText: Conduction transfers heat through...

checkOptions.text: Particles physically travelling to a new location
Empty space with no particles at all

chunks.heading: Conductors and insulators
chunks.body: A conductor lets heat pass through it easily, like metal. An insulator resists the flow of heat, like wood or foam.
chunks.checkText: An insulator is a material that...

checkOptions.text: Lets heat pass through very easily

chunks.heading: What speeds up conduction
chunks.body: Heat conducts faster through a material with a bigger temperature difference, a thinner layer, or a larger area. Good conductors also speed up the process.
chunks.checkText: Which of these would speed up conduction through a wall?

checkOptions.text: Cooling both sides to the same temperature

chunks.heading: Convection
chunks.body: Convection transfers heat through a fluid as warm, less dense regions rise and cool, denser regions sink. This creates a circulating current that spreads heat through the whole fluid.
chunks.checkText: Convection relies on...

checkOptions.text: Warm fluid rising and cool fluid sinking
Electromagnetic waves travelling through a vacuum

chunks.heading: Radiation: heat without a medium
chunks.body: Radiation transfers heat as electromagnetic waves, so unlike conduction and convection, it needs no medium at all. This is how the Sun's energy reaches Earth through empty space.
chunks.checkText: Unlike conduction and convection, radiation can transfer heat...

checkOptions.text: Through empty space, with no medium needed

chunks.heading: What affects radiation absorption
chunks.body: Dark, matt surfaces absorb and emit radiant heat faster than light, shiny surfaces. This is why a dark car interior heats up faster in the sun than a light one.
chunks.checkText: A dark, matt surface absorbs and emits radiant heat...

checkOptions.text: Faster than a light, shiny surface
Slower than a light, shiny surface
At exactly the same rate as any surface
